cards.q: What is the general formula of the alkenes (with one C=C double bond)?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}\)
cards.why: For example ethene \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}\), propene \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}}\) and butene \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}\).

cards.q: Why are alkenes described as unsaturated hydrocarbons?
cards.a: They contain only carbon and hydrogen, and they have a carbon–carbon double bond, so more atoms can be added to them.
cards.why: Saturated means only single bonds, as in the alkanes.

cards.q: Give the molecular formula of cyclohexene, and say why it does not fit the general formula of the alkenes.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of cyclohexene: a six-membered carbon ring with one C=C double bond.

cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{10}}\). The ring removes two more hydrogens, so cycloalkenes have the general formula \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n-2}}\).
cards.why: Cyclohexene is still unsaturated: it decolourises bromine water just like an open-chain alkene.

cards.q: Describe the bonding in the C=C double bond in terms of σ- and π-bonds.
cards.a: One σ-bond, formed by head-on (end-on) overlap of orbitals between the nuclei, and one π-bond, formed by sideways overlap of p-orbitals, above and below the plane of the σ-bond.
cards.why: The π-bond’s electron density lies outside the line between the two nuclei.

cards.q: Explain why alkenes are much more reactive than alkanes.
cards.a: The C=C bond is a region of high electron density, and its π-bond is weak.
marks: The C=C double bond is a centre of high electron density, which attracts electrophiles.
The π-electrons lie above and below the plane of the bond, exposed to attack.
The π-bond is weaker than a σ-bond (less overlap), so it breaks more easily.

cards.q: Z-but-2-ene (shown) and E-but-2-ene are isomers. Why can one not turn into the other at room temperature?

figure.alt: Z-but-2-ene: the two methyl groups are on the same side of the C=C double bond.

answerFigure.alt: E-but-2-ene: the two methyl groups are on opposite sides of the C=C double bond.

cards.a: The π-bond prevents rotation about the C=C double bond: rotating would mean breaking the π-bond.
cards.why: This restricted rotation is why E/Z isomers exist. The answer shows E-but-2-ene, with the methyl groups on opposite sides.

cards.q: What is an electrophile?
cards.a: An electron pair acceptor: a species attracted to a region of high electron density.
cards.why: Examples: \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), the \(\delta+\) H of HBr, and the \(\delta+\) end of a polarised \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) molecule.

cards.q: What is heterolytic fission, and what does it form?
cards.a: Breaking a covalent bond so that both bonding electrons go to one atom. It forms a positive ion and a negative ion.
cards.why: In homolytic fission one electron goes to each atom, forming two radicals.

cards.q: True or false: when H–Br reacts with an alkene, the H–Br bond breaks homolytically.
cards.a: False. It breaks heterolytically: both electrons go to the bromine, forming a bromide ion.
cards.why: Electrophilic addition is an ionic mechanism, shown with full (two-electron) curly arrows.

cards.q: How is an alkene converted into an alkane?
cards.a: Heat with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst (about 150 °C).

answerFigure.alt: Ethene reacts with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst at about 150 °C to give ethane.

cards.why: Hydrogen adds across the double bond, so the product is saturated.

cards.q: How is hydrogenation used to make margarine, and why does it work?
cards.a: Unsaturated vegetable oils are partially hydrogenated with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst. Removing some C=C bonds raises the melting point, so the oil becomes a soft solid that spreads.
cards.why: With fewer double bonds the chains are straighter, pack more closely, and have stronger London forces between them.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethene with bromine, and name the product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{2}=CH_{2} + Br_{2} \rightarrow CH_{2}BrCH_{2}Br}\)
1,2-dibromoethane

answerFigure.alt: Ethene reacts with bromine at room temperature to give 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.why: One bromine atom adds to each carbon of the double bond.

cards.q: Describe the test for a C=C double bond.
cards.a: Add bromine water and shake. An alkene turns it from orange to colourless.
cards.why: Bromine adds across the C=C bond. An alkane leaves the bromine water orange.

cards.q: You have two colourless liquids, cyclohexane and cyclohexene. How could you tell them apart?
cards.a: Shake each with bromine water. Cyclohexene decolourises it (orange to colourless); cyclohexane does not.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of cyclohexene: a six-membered carbon ring with one C=C double bond.

cards.why: Only cyclohexene has a C=C double bond. Both are cyclic, so the ring makes no difference.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethene with hydrogen bromide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{2}=CH_{2} + HBr \rightarrow  CH_{3}CH_{2}Br}\)

answerFigure.alt: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide at room temperature to give bromoethane.

cards.why: The product is bromoethane, a halogenoalkane.

cards.q: What is formed when an alkene reacts with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst?
cards.a: An alcohol: for example, ethene gives ethanol.

answerFigure.alt: Ethene reacts with steam, with a phosphoric acid catalyst, to give ethanol.

cards.why: \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CH_{2} + H_{2}O \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}OH}\). Industrially the catalyst is phosphoric acid.

cards.q: What is formed when ethene reacts with acidified potassium manganate(VII), and what is seen?
cards.a: Ethane-1,2-diol, which has an OH group on each carbon. The solution changes from purple to colourless.

answerFigure.alt: Ethene is oxidised by acidified potassium manganate(VII) to ethane-1,2-diol, which has an OH group on each carbon.

cards.why: The C=C bond is oxidised. With [O]: \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CH_{2} + H_{2}O + [O] \rightarrow HOCH_{2}CH_{2}OH}\).

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethene with cold, concentrated sulfuric acid, and name the product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{2}=CH_{2} + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}OSO_{2}OH}\)
Ethyl hydrogensulfate

answerFigure.alt: Ethene reacts with cold concentrated sulfuric acid to give ethyl hydrogensulfate, CH3CH2OSO2OH.

cards.why: The H adds to one carbon and the \(\mathrm{OSO_{2}OH}\) group to the other.

cards.q: How is ethyl hydrogensulfate converted into ethanol, and what is the role of sulfuric acid overall?
cards.a: Warm it with water: it is hydrolysed to ethanol and sulfuric acid. Sulfuric acid is regenerated, so overall it is a catalyst for adding water to ethene.

answerFigure.alt: Ethyl hydrogensulfate is warmed with water to give ethanol and sulfuric acid.

cards.why: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OSO_{2}OH + H_{2}O \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + H_{2}SO_{4}}\)

cards.q: What type of reaction mechanism do alkenes undergo with HBr, bromine and sulfuric acid?
cards.a: Electrophilic addition.
cards.why: An electrophile attacks the C=C bond, and two groups add across it to give a single product.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethene with hydrogen bromide.
cards.a: Electrophilic addition, through a carbocation.

answerFigure.alt: Electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene. The C=C bond attacks the δ+ hydrogen of HBr and the H–Br bond breaks, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion; the bromide ion’s lone pair then attacks the positive carbon, giving bromoethane.

marks: A curly arrow from the C=C bond to the \(\delta+\) H of H–Br (with \(\delta+\)/\(\delta-\) shown on H–Br).
A curly arrow from the H–Br bond to the Br atom, giving \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\).
The carbocation intermediate, with the + charge on the carbon that did not gain H.
A curly arrow from a lone pair on \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) to the positive carbon.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethene with bromine.
cards.a: Electrophilic addition: the bromine molecule is polarised as it approaches.

answerFigure.alt: Electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene. The C=C bond attacks the δ+ bromine of the polarised Br2 molecule and the Br–Br bond breaks, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion, which then attacks the carbocation to give 1,2-dibromoethane.

marks: The C=C bond induces a dipole in \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\): \(\mathrm{Br^{\delta+}}\)–\(\mathrm{Br^{\delta-}}\).
Curly arrows from the C=C bond to the \(\delta+\) Br, and from the Br–Br bond to the \(\delta-\) Br.
A carbocation with Br on the other carbon; then a curly arrow from a lone pair on \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) to the C+, giving 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.q: Bromine, \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\), is a non-polar molecule. Explain how it can act as an electrophile.
cards.a: The alkene induces a dipole in it.
marks: As the bromine molecule approaches the C=C bond, the high electron density repels the electrons in the Br–Br bond.
This induces a dipole: the Br nearer the alkene becomes \(\delta+\), the other \(\delta-\).
The \(\delta+\) Br accepts a pair of electrons from the C=C bond.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethene with concentrated sulfuric acid.
cards.a: Electrophilic addition: a δ+ H of the acid is the electrophile.

answerFigure.alt: Electrophilic addition of sulfuric acid to ethene. The C=C bond attacks a δ+ hydrogen of H2SO4 and the O–H bond breaks, giving a carbocation and a hydrogensulfate ion, whose oxygen lone pair attacks the carbocation to give ethyl hydrogensulfate.

marks: A curly arrow from the C=C bond to a \(\delta+\) H of \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\), and from the O–H bond to the O.
A carbocation and the hydrogensulfate ion, \(\mathrm{^{-}OSO_{2}OH}\), form.
A curly arrow from a lone pair on an O of \(\mathrm{^{-}OSO_{2}OH}\) to the C+, giving \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OSO_{2}OH}\).

cards.q: In this mechanism, where must the first curly arrow start and end?

figure.alt: Electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene. The C=C bond attacks the δ+ hydrogen of HBr and the H–Br bond breaks, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion; the bromide ion’s lone pair then attacks the positive carbon, giving bromoethane.

cards.a: It starts at the C=C double bond (the \(\pi\)-electrons) and ends at the \(\delta+\) hydrogen atom of HBr.
cards.why: A curly arrow shows a pair of electrons moving: here from the double bond to form a new C–H bond.

cards.q: True or false: in electrophilic addition, the first curly arrow can start from one of the carbon atoms of the double bond.
cards.a: False. It must start from the double bond itself.
cards.why: The electrons that attack the electrophile are the π-bond electrons, between the two carbons, not on one atom.

cards.q: Iodine monochloride, \(\mathrm{ICl}\), adds to ethene by the same mechanism as bromine. Outline the mechanism and name the product.
cards.a: Electrophilic addition; the product is 1-chloro-2-iodoethane.

answerFigure.alt: Electrophilic addition of iodine monochloride to ethene. Iodine is the δ+ end; the C=C bond attacks the iodine and the I–Cl bond breaks, giving a carbocation and a chloride ion, which attacks to give 1-chloro-2-iodoethane.

marks: Chlorine is more electronegative than iodine, so I is \(\delta+\) and Cl is \(\delta-\).
Curly arrows from the C=C bond to the I, and from the I–Cl bond to the Cl.
A curly arrow from a lone pair on \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) to the carbocation, giving \(\mathrm{CH_{2}ClCH_{2}I}\).

cards.q: Put primary, secondary and tertiary carbocations in order of stability.

figure.alt: Three carbocations: CH3CH2 plus (primary, one alkyl group on the positive carbon), (CH3)2CH plus (secondary, two alkyl groups) and (CH3)3C plus (tertiary, three alkyl groups).

cards.a: Tertiary > secondary > primary (most stable first).
cards.why: The more alkyl groups bonded to the positive carbon, the more stable the carbocation.

cards.q: Explain why a tertiary carbocation is more stable than a primary carbocation.
cards.a: More alkyl groups push electron density onto the positive carbon.
marks: Alkyl groups are electron-releasing (they have a positive inductive effect).
A tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups on the positive carbon; a primary has only one.
So the positive charge is spread out (stabilised) more in the tertiary carbocation.

cards.q: Classify this carbocation as primary, secondary or tertiary.

figure.alt: A carbocation: a positively charged carbon bonded to a methyl group, an ethyl group and a hydrogen atom.

cards.a: Secondary.
cards.why: The positive carbon is bonded to two alkyl groups (methyl and ethyl) and one hydrogen.

cards.q: Propene reacts with HBr. Name the major product and explain, with the mechanism, why it is the major product.
cards.a: 2-bromopropane.

answerFigure.alt: Electrophilic addition of HBr to propene giving the major product. The hydrogen adds to the CH2 end, so the positive charge is on the middle carbon (a secondary carbocation); bromide then attacks it, giving 2-bromopropane.

marks: H adds to the end carbon (CH₂), giving a secondary carbocation on the middle carbon.
The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation that the other way round would give.
So it forms faster and in greater amount; \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) then attacks it to give 2-bromopropane.

cards.q: Propene reacts with HBr to give a minor product as well. Name it and say why only a little forms.
cards.a: 1-bromopropane. It forms through a primary carbocation, which is less stable, so this route is much less likely.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of 1-bromopropane: a three-carbon chain with bromine on an end carbon.

cards.why: Major and minor products come from the two different carbocations an unsymmetrical alkene can form.

cards.q: This alkene reacts with hydrogen bromide. Give the name of the major product.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-methylpropene: a C=C double bond with two methyl groups on one carbon and two hydrogens on the other.

cards.a: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: a central carbon bonded to three methyl groups and a bromine atom.

cards.why: Adding H to the CH₂ end gives a tertiary carbocation, the most stable kind; the minor product, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, comes from a primary carbocation.

cards.q: Propene reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid and the product is then warmed with water. Which alcohol is the main product?
cards.a: Propan-2-ol.
cards.why: The H adds to the CH₂ end, giving the more stable secondary carbocation, so the hydrogensulfate group (then OH) ends up on the middle carbon.

cards.q: True or false: the major product forms because hydrogen simply prefers to join the carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms.
cards.a: False. That is only a pattern. The reason is the stability of the carbocation intermediate.
cards.why: Exam answers must refer to the relative stability of the primary, secondary or tertiary carbocations.

cards.q: But-1-ene reacts with HBr. Name the major product.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of but-1-ene: a four-carbon chain with the double bond between carbons 1 and 2.

cards.a: 2-bromobutane.
cards.why: H adds to carbon 1, giving a secondary carbocation on carbon 2, rather than a primary one on carbon 1.

cards.q: Name the product when propene reacts with bromine.
cards.a: 1,2-dibromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₂Br.
cards.why: Both atoms added are the same, so there is only one product: no major and minor products here.

cards.q: An alkene with one C=C bond has \(M_{\text{r}} = 70.0\). Find its molecular formula. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): C 12.0, H 1.0)
cards.why: Pentene has five carbons and ten hydrogens.

cards.q: 0.0100 mol of an unsaturated hydrocarbon reacts completely with 3.20 g of bromine, \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) (\(M_{\text{r}} = 159.8\)). How many C=C bonds does each molecule contain?
cards.a: 2
steps: One \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) adds across each C=C bond, so there are 2 C=C bonds.
cards.why: This is how the degree of unsaturation of a fat or oil can be measured.

cards.q: What is an addition polymer?
cards.a: A long-chain molecule formed when many monomer molecules with a C=C double bond join together, with no other product.
cards.why: Addition polymers are made from alkenes and substituted alkenes.

cards.q: Draw the repeating unit of the polymer made from propene.
cards.a: Poly(propene): two carbons in the chain, one carrying a methyl group, with bonds sticking out of the brackets on both sides.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(propene): two carbons in brackets with bonds extending out on both sides; one carbon has two hydrogens, the other a hydrogen and a methyl group; subscript n.

cards.why: The C=C double bond opens to a single bond, and the methyl group becomes a side branch.

cards.q: Here is a section of a polymer chain. Give the name of the monomer and of the polymer.

figure.alt: Displayed formula of a section of a polymer chain: six carbons in a row, bonds continuing at both ends; every carbon has a hydrogen above it, and alternate carbons have a hydrogen or a chlorine below.

cards.a: Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl, which forms poly(chloroethene) (PVC).

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(chloroethene): two carbons in brackets with bonds extending out; one carbon has two hydrogens, the other a hydrogen and a chlorine atom; subscript n.

cards.why: The repeating unit is two carbons long: find it, then put back the C=C bond.

cards.q: Name the addition polymer made from this monomer.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of phenylethene: a benzene ring bonded to a CH=CH2 group.

cards.a: Poly(phenylethene) (polystyrene).
cards.why: IUPAC rule: put the monomer’s name in brackets after “poly”.

cards.q: This is the repeating unit of a polymer. Name the monomer and the polymer.

figure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(tetrafluoroethene): two carbons in brackets with bonds extending out, each carbon bonded to two fluorine atoms; subscript n.

cards.a: Tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂, which forms poly(tetrafluoroethene) (PTFE).
cards.why: Join the two carbons of the repeating unit with a double bond and remove the bonds out of the brackets.

cards.q: Explain why addition polymers are unreactive.
cards.a: Their chains are saturated, held together by strong, non-polar bonds.
marks: The C=C bonds of the monomer have become single bonds, so the polymer is saturated (like an alkane).
The C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar, so they are not attacked by electrophiles or nucleophiles.

cards.q: True or false: poly(ethene) decolourises bromine water because it is made from ethene.
cards.a: False. Poly(ethene) has no C=C double bonds, so it does not react.
cards.why: The double bonds are used up in polymerisation; the name keeps “ethene” only to show the monomer.

cards.q: Explain the intermolecular forces between the chains of a polyalkene such as poly(ethene), and why they are strong overall.
cards.a: Van der Waals forces (London forces) between very long chains.
marks: The chains are non-polar, so the forces between them are van der Waals forces (induced dipole–dipole).
The chains are very long, with many electrons and a large area of contact.
So the total attraction between chains is large, making the polymer a solid.

cards.q: Why are the forces between chains in poly(chloroethene) stronger than in poly(ethene) of similar chain length?
cards.a: The polar C–Cl bonds give permanent dipole–dipole forces between the chains, as well as van der Waals forces.
cards.why: This is why unplasticised PVC is hard and rigid.

cards.q: How does a plasticiser change the properties of PVC, and how is each form used?
cards.a: It makes PVC flexible.
marks: Plasticiser molecules fit between the polymer chains and push them apart.
This weakens the forces between chains, so they slide over each other: the PVC becomes flexible.
Rigid (unplasticised) PVC: window frames and drainpipes. Plasticised PVC: electrical cable insulation and flooring.
